activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Ruby went to the garden center with Dad. She wanted to grow her own vegetables. There were so many plants to pick. "Look at this one," said Ruby. She held up a small tomato plant. It had one tiny green leaf on top.

Ruby put the plant in her cart. She also got a little carrot seed packet. Dad got a big bag of soil. At home, Dad filled a pot with soil. Ruby made a small hole with her hand. She set the tomato plant in. She patted the soil down. Then Ruby dropped three carrot seeds in a second pot. She covered them with soft soil.

Ruby watered both pots. She put them by the sunny window. Every morning she looked. "Nothing yet," said Ruby. Then one day, a small green leaf popped up. "Dad, come see!" Ruby called. Dad came fast. More leaves came, one by one. The noisy cat next door meowed at the window. "Look, cat," said Ruby. "My plant grew!" She gave the plant more water. The carrot leaves grew tall and feathery. Ruby counted them with her finger. Then she smiled and whispered, "Grow, little plant, grow."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Carter wanted to help make breakfast. Mom said, "Stay here by me." Carter stood close to Mom's legs. He could see the stove from there.

The pan sat on the stove. It made a sizzle sound. Steam went up, up, up. Carter wondered, was the pan hot or cold? He put his hand near it. The air felt warm. Mom moved his hand back. "The pan is hot," she said. "Only grown-ups touch it." Carter nodded. He looked at his toy pig on the floor. The pig was different. The pig stayed cold.

"Can I help a safe way?" asked Carter. Mom gave him a cold spoon. Carter stirred the eggs in a bowl. The spoon went round and round. Mom poured the eggs into the pan. Sizzle, sizzle!

The eggs turned from runny to fluffy. Carter saw that the hot pan had done that. "Breakfast is ready," said Mom. Carter clapped and hugged his pig.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum. He wanted to make it sound big.

Felix tapped it with one finger. The drum went tap, tap. That was too small. He waited. Then he tapped with his whole hand. The drum went boom. A big sound came out! Felix tapped again and again. Boom, boom, boom.

Miss Ana smiled. "You made a big sound," she said. "Do it once more, slowly." Felix raised his hand high. He waited a moment. Then his hand came down. Boom. The sound was so big that a bird outside the window flew up into the sky.

Felix laughed. He looked at his hand. Then he looked at the drum. He lifted his hand one more time and said, "Boom."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Milo went to the library with his mom. He found a book about a big red fire truck. He opened the front of the book. The words ran one way, all the way to the back. Milo put his finger under the words. "That says fire truck," his mom said. Milo tapped the word. The page showed a fire truck. The words made the picture come.

"I want to keep it forever," said Milo. He held the book tight.

The library lady shook her head. "The book goes back," she said. "Someone else wants to read it too." She held up a small card. The card had a day on it. "Bring the book back on this day."

Milo looked at the card. He did not want to let go.

At home, Milo read the fire truck book every day. He read it front to back. He read it under the tree in the yard. He read it while the busy birds chirped outside.

Then the card day came. Milo carried the book back to the library. He set it on the desk. A girl picked it up right away. She opened the front cover.

"Fire truck," Milo said, pointing at the word.

The girl smiled and turned the first page.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Logan held Daddy's hand at the hotel pool. The water was blue and cool. "I want to swim," said Logan. "I might sink down." Daddy held him close. "I have you," said Daddy.

Logan kicked his legs. He blew bubbles in the water. Then he saw a little pink ball float by. It sat on top of the water. It did not sink at all! Logan let go of Daddy's thumb and put his hand out. He pushed the ball down. The ball popped right back up. It floated again.

Logan lay back in Daddy's arms. His tummy went up, like the ball. His ears were in the water. He heard a swishy sound. "I float!" said Logan. Daddy smiled. "Yes, you float," said Daddy. Logan saw the pink ball bobbing next to him, right there by his cute toes.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Cooper was going to the big game! Dad held his hand. Aunt Mei carried hot cocoa. Cooper wore his red robot hat.

The ice rink was loud and bright. The skaters zoomed past. "Go, go, go!" shouted Cooper. But his team was losing. Cooper felt small in the big crowd.

Then Cooper saw something. When he clapped his mittens, the man next to him clapped too. Clap, clap! When Cooper stomped his feet, Aunt Mei stomped too. Stomp, stomp! Soon everyone was clapping and stomping. The noise grew and grew. The players skated faster and faster. His team scored a goal!

"That was so loud!" said Dad. "The smelly old rink smelled like popcorn," said Aunt Mei, "and it was the best game ever."

"Did you see that?" asked Cooper. "I started the clapping!"

story:
Grayson ran to the playground with his mama. The sun was hot on his face. The slide was hot too. He put his hand near it and pulled it back fast.

"Too hot," said Mama. "Let's find the shady slide." Grayson touched the shady slide. It felt cool. He slid down, down, down. "Again!" he said. He slid again and again.

Then Grayson saw a shiny thing in the grass. It was a piece of glass. It sparkled in the sun. He reached out his hand. Mama came quickly and picked it up with her glove. "Not for touching," she said. She put it far away in a bin. Grayson waved bye-bye to the glass.

Next, Grayson saw a picnic table. A man was eating pizza there. The cheese was bubbly and hot. Grayson stood far away and watched. The man blew on his slice. He blew and blew. Then he took a little bite. Grayson held Mama's hand the whole time.

"Stay close," said Mama. Grayson stayed close. They walked to the swings together. The swing went up, and the swing went down. Grayson laughed. "One more push, Mama!" he said.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay at Jaxon's house. He would stay for a whole week. Jaxon wanted to make Grandpa laugh every day.

In the backyard, Jaxon found his rubber snake. It was long and green. "What does this snake do?" Jaxon asked. Grandpa smiled. "Watch," he said. Grandpa put the snake in the grass. Then he called, "Grandma, come look!"

But Grandpa had a trick of his own. He hid the snake under Jaxon's sand bucket. When Jaxon lifted the bucket, the snake popped out. Jaxon jumped. "You made me jump!" he said. Grandpa laughed and laughed.

The next day, Jaxon tried the trick too. He put the snake by the door. Grandpa opened the door. He jumped up high. "I am afraid of snakes!" Grandpa said. Jaxon laughed so hard. "The snake made you jump!" he said. "My turn again," said Grandpa, and he picked up the green snake.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Sienna's hair was in her eyes. Grandma brushed it. It fell right back. "We need a haircut," said Grandma. "A real one, at the salon." Sienna held Grandma's hand tight. She did not want the scissors near her head.

At the salon, a lady named Roz put a cape on Sienna. The cape was blue and shiny. Roz picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. Little pieces of hair fell down. They landed on the cape. They made a small pile. The pile grew and grew. Now it looked like a tiny mountain on Sienna's lap. "Look at that," said Grandma. "You grew a hair mountain!"

Sienna laughed. She wanted a bigger mountain. "More, please," she said. Roz snipped some more. The mountain grew taller. Then Roz spun the chair around. Sienna saw a girl in the mirror. The girl had short hair. She could see her eyes! "That's me," said Sienna. She waved at the girl. The girl waved back. "Bye bye, hair mountain," said Sienna.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Jacob skipped into the kitchen. The table was set for dinner. His bowl was red. Mama's bowl was big. Papa's plate was white.

"Can we eat now?" Jacob asked.

"First we hold hands," said Papa. "Then we say our thank you."

Jacob wanted his noodles. They smelled warm and good. But he put his little hand in Mama's big hand. He put his other hand in Papa's hand.

"Now we all close our eyes," said Mama. Jacob squeezed his eyes shut. The kitchen went dark behind his eyelids.

"Thank you for this food," said Papa.

"Thank you for our day," said Mama.

"Thank you for noodles," said Jacob. He peeked with one eye. Everyone was still holding hands.

They opened their eyes. They smiled at each other. Then they ate!

"Tomorrow we say it again," said Jacob.

"Yes," said Mama. "One family, two hands, three bowls."

Jacob looked at the window. "Look, snow!" The white flakes fell past the glass, and he waved his spoon at them.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Oliver walked home with a small box. Inside was his first pet, a little puppy. The puppy was brown and soft.

On the street, the puppy made a sad sound. "He is whining," said Mom. Oliver peeked in the box. The puppy licked his hand. "He likes you," said Mom. At home, Oliver put the puppy on the floor. The puppy walked around and around. Then he nosed his empty water bowl.

"Mom, the bowl is empty!" said Oliver. Mom held the bowl, and Oliver poured in fresh water. The puppy ran to the bowl. He drank and drank. Then his tail went wag, wag, wag. "You were thirsty," said Oliver. He patted the puppy's nice soft ears. The puppy gave his shoe a little chew. "No, that would hurt my toe," said Oliver, and he gave the puppy a bone instead. The puppy lay down with his bone and looked up at Oliver. "Good boy," said Oliver.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Florence ran to the shape wall at school. It had a circle, a square, and a rectangle. But the triangle spot was empty! "We need a triangle," said her teacher. "Can you help find one?"

Florence looked all around. The clock was round like a circle. The window was a square with four sides. The door was a tall rectangle. "Pay attention, triangle," she whispered. "Come out!" Then she looked out the window. A bird flew to a nest in the tree. The nest sat on top of the little wooden birdhouse. The birdhouse roof had three sides and three points!

"There you are!" Florence cried. She pointed and pointed. Her teacher came to look. "Yes! A triangle roof," she said. Florence clapped her hands. The bird was safe in its nest. Florence drew the triangle all by herself. She ran back and taped it on the empty spot. The shape wall was full at last. "Look, look!" said Florence. "Now it is done!"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
story:
Charlie woke up and looked out the window. Snow was everywhere. Snow on the road. Snow on the cars. Snow on the trees. "A snow day!" said Mama. "No school today."

Charlie put on his boots. He put on his big coat. He went outside with Mama. Charlie wanted to make a snowman. He patted the snow. He patted and patted. The snow got round. The snow got big. His pats made the snow stick together.

Then Charlie saw something. When he stomped his boot, snow fell off the tree. Stomp, and down it came. He stomped again. More snow fell on his hat. A little snow went in his ear. Charlie laughed. He stomped by the empty mailbox too, but that snow did not fall. Only the tree snow fell.

Charlie peeked up at the branches. He stomped one more time. The last bit of snow came down like a soft white hat. "Goodbye, tree snow," said Charlie. He waved at the tree and held Mama's hand.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Carter sat on the big soft rug. Everyone came to watch the game. Mama was there. Papa was there. Uncle Ben was there too. The room smelled like warm popcorn.

The game was close. Papa waved his arms. Uncle Ben jumped up. Carter wanted to see better. He clapped his hands. Then everyone clapped too. Carter stomped his feet on the floor. Then Uncle Ben stomped too. Carter blew a big breath. Mama blew one too. Each thing Carter did, the big people did after him.

Carter looked at the clock. Then he stood very still. He put one finger on his nose. The room went quiet. Everyone put a finger on a nose. Then Carter giggled, and everyone giggled. The team on the screen scored a point. "We win!" said Papa. "Thank you, Carter," said Mama. "You are a different kind of cheerleader." Carter took a deep bow.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Jasper sat at the table. Daddy put a orange on his plate.

"Let's play a game," said Daddy. "What do your eyes do?"

Jasper looked at the orange. "My eyes see it! It is bright and orange."

"Good! Now close your eyes."

Jasper squeezed his eyes shut. He could not see the orange. But he could hear something. Snip, snip, snip. Daddy was peeling it.

"My ears hear that!" said Jasper.

"Good try," said Daddy. He held out his hand. "What is this?"

Jasper touched it. It was bumpy and cold. "My hands feel it!" he said. "Wait. My skin feels it!"

Daddy smiled. He put a piece of orange near Jasper's nose. Jasper sniffed. It smelled sweet. "My nose smells it!"

"Now open your mouth."

Jasper took a bite. Yum! It was juicy. "My tongue tastes it!" he said.

Jasper wanted to do one more thing. He stood up. He wanted to swing his arms like a big wind. He swung and swung. Then he hit his cup, and it tipped over. Milk ran across the table.

"Oh no!" said Jasper.

Daddy ran over with a towel. "That is okay," he said. "We can wipe it up. Mistakes happen when we learn."

Jasper helped wipe the milk. Then he had an idea. He picked up one small piece of orange. He held it out to the cat.

The cat sniffed it with her little nose. Then she turned away.

"Cats do not like oranges," laughed Jasper.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Ruby went to the doctor with her mama. She wanted to know why her neck felt sore. "The doctor will look at you," said Mama.

First the doctor looked in Ruby's eyes. "I see you blinking!" she said. Then Ruby heard a beep. It was a little machine. "My ears heard that!" said Ruby. The doctor let Ruby touch a soft teddy bear. It was fuzzy on her fingers. Ruby smelled something sweet. A sticker smelled like strawberries! She stuck out her tongue. "I taste apple juice," said Ruby, because Mama gave her a sip.

Then the doctor said, "Turn your head." Ruby turned her neck, slowly, slowly. It did not hurt now! "You did it," said Mama, and she clapped. Ruby put the sweet sticker on her shirt. "Next time I want to do it again," said Ruby.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Joseph ran to the window at school. The sun was out. "It is sunny today," said Miss Kim. Joseph wanted to play outside.

Joseph put on his sun hat. Then he heard a sound. Drip, drip, drip. Rain fell on the window. "Now it is rainy," said Miss Kim. Joseph put his hat away. He reached for his rain boots and his rain coat.

Outside, the wind blew. "It is windy too," laughed Joseph. His hat flew off. Miss Kim caught it. She put it in her pocket. "Your family gave you warm clothes," she said. Joseph felt a cold spot on his nose. Small white flakes fell down. "Snow!" said Joseph.

"Snow means mittens," said Miss Kim. She pulled warm mittens from the box. Joseph held out his hands. "Now my hands stay awake and warm," he said. Miss Kim laughed. They made white footprints side by side in the snow.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Penelope went out to the backyard. She wanted to find something red. She looked by the big tree. She saw green grass and green leaves. No red yet.

Then she heard a little buzz. A bee flew to a yellow flower. The bee sat on the yellow flower. Then it flew to a blue flower too. Penelope watched the bee go from flower to flower.

The bee dropped some yellow dust. The dust fell on Penelope's red apple. The apple sat on the clean table by her chair. Yellow dust made little dots on the red apple. Penelope laughed. Her red apple had yellow spots now.

Dad came out with a broom. He began to sweep the leaves off the patio. Penelope showed him the apple. "Look, Dad. Yellow dots on red," she said. Dad smiled and nodded. The bee buzzed by one more time, then went home to its hive.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Livia ran to the door when Mommy said, "Doctor day!" Livia loved the doctor's office. It had stickers and a fish tank. She wanted a dinosaur sticker next.

In the big room, the nurse said, "Time for your shot." Livia looked at her arm. She squeezed her teddy bear tight. "One little pin," said the nurse. The nurse pushed the tiny needle in. "Ow!" said Livia. Then it was done. "All done," said the nurse.

"Look, Mommy, look!" cried Livia. There was a small red dot on her arm. Mommy kissed the dot. Livia kissed her teddy bear's arm too. The nurse laughed and held out a basket. There were no dinosaur stickers. There was a shiny bandage with stars. "Stars for a brave girl," said the nurse. Livia stuck the bandage right next to the red dot and smiled.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Cooper ran onto the soccer field. His team wore blue shirts today. He wanted to score one goal this season. He had not scored yet.

The coach gave him a drink of water. "Go get the ball, Cooper," she said. Cooper kicked the ball. It went a little way and stopped. He kicked it again. It rolled more. Then Cooper saw it. When he ran fast, the ball rolled fast too. When he ran slow, the ball rolled slow. He ran fast, and the ball rolled fast all the way down the field.

The grass was pretty and green in the sun. Cooper kicked the ball toward the net. The ball went in! The blue team cheered loud. "I did it!" Cooper said. Then he picked up the ball and hugged it tight.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
It was Hudson's birthday at the bowling alley. Mom gave him a big red ball. He wanted to knock down all the pins.

Hudson pushed the ball. It went slow. The pins did not fall down. "Oh no," said Hudson. "That is a problem." Dad knelt beside him. "Push it fast this time," Dad said. "You are safe here. Just watch."

Hudson drew his arm back far. Then he pushed the ball fast. The ball rolled and rolled. It hit the pins. All ten pins fell down with a big crash! Everyone clapped. His friends jumped up and down.

Then the lights went dim. Mom carried a cake with three little candles. Mom blew out the candles, and the smoke curled up. Hudson got the first big slice. "Happy birthday, Hudson!" everyone sang. Hudson took a huge bite of cake.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Jaxon sat in the car with Mom. The car went past the egg shop. The car went past the big park. The car went past the yellow bus. "We are going to get your first haircut," said Mom. Jaxon held his toy truck. He did not want his hair cut.

At the salon, a lady named Rosa smiled at him. She put a soft cape on Jaxon. Then she picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Jaxon watched the mirror. The scissors cut his hair. Then the little hairs fell down. Snip, then fall. Snip, then fall. They landed on the cape like tiny bits of string.

Jaxon pointed at the little hairs. "Look, Mom! The scissors make the hairs come down!" He turned his head to see. More hairs fell. Rosa laughed softly. She let Jaxon hold the little brush. He helped her brush the hairs off the chair. One sweep, two sweeps, three sweeps.

Then Rosa turned on a warm fan. It made warm air. The warm air made Jaxon's hair dry and soft. It made his head feel like sunshine. Rosa held up the mirror. Jaxon saw a boy with short, neat hair. The boy looked happy. "That's me!" said Jaxon. Mom hugged him tight. On the ride home, the sun did shine on his new hair. "Egg shop, park, bus," said Jaxon, looking out the window. Then he fell fast asleep.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Rosalie ran to the paint table. Three big pots sat there. One pot was red. One pot was yellow. One pot was blue.

"I want to paint a sun," said Rosalie. "The sun is yellow. Yellow is my best one!" She dipped her brush. She painted a big yellow circle.

Then she stopped. She wanted to paint an orange too. But there was no orange paint. She looked in all the pots. Red, yellow, blue. No orange anywhere. "Oh no," said Rosalie. She put her brush down.

Her teacher sat beside her. "Try your brush in the red," she said. Rosalie dipped her brush in the red pot. She painted red on top of her yellow circle. She stirred it round and round with her brush.

The circle turned orange! "Look, look!" said Rosalie. "It is a true orange now!" She held up her paper. Then she ran to the shelf to get more paper. She was going to paint one in every colour she could make. "I will paint a green apple next," she said. Her teacher handed her the blue pot.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Lena found a red book at daycare. It was about a spoon who loved soup. On the cover, Lena saw little marks. "What are those?" she asked.

"They are words," said Ben. "My mom reads them to me."

Miss Tia sat down. She held the book. She opened the front page first. She turned each page, one by one. Lena listened. The spoon jumped into the pot. Lena laughed.

"Again!" she said.

"You can take it home," said Miss Tia. "It is a library book. But on Friday, it comes back. Other kids want to read it too."

Lena hugged the book. At home, Dad read it twice. Lena kicked her feet with joy.

On Friday, Lena put the book in her bag. At daycare, Ben held it. "Now I read it," he said.

Lena patted the cover. "The spoon is sharp and funny," she said. "Read it to me too."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Naomi had a beautiful library book about a little red dragon. She wanted to keep it forever. At bedtime she hugged the book tight. "Mine," she whispered.

But Mama said, "Tomorrow is take-back day." Naomi frowned. She looked at the cover. The cover had words on it. The words said the dragon's name was Pip. Naomi pointed at the words. Mama read them out loud. Words could talk! Naomi turned page one, then page two, then page three. The dragon story went from the front to the back. She counted, "One, two, three, four, five pages left."

The next morning they went to the library. Naomi gave the book to the lady at the desk. Then the lady gave it back for one last hug, and put it on the shelf. "Goodbye, Pip," said Naomi. Then she chose a new book, all about a big blue whale. "This one goes front to back too," she said. "I checked."

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Florence stood in the backyard. Dad put a red hoop on the grass. "Throw the beanbag in," said Dad. Florence threw it. The beanbag hit the rim. It fell out. "Try again," said Dad. Florence held the beanbag up high. She looked at the hole in the middle. She let it go. The beanbag dropped through the hoop. It landed in the grass with a soft plop.

"Now catch the big ball," said Dad. He blew a little puff of air and rolled the ball to her. Florence held out one hand. The ball bumped her fingers. It bounced away. The dog ran after it and fell asleep on the ball, like it was a pillow.

"No, silly dog," said Florence. She used both hands to pull the ball out. Dad rolled it again. This time Florence held out two hands, cupped like a little soup bowl. The ball landed right in them. She did not drop it.

"I caught it!" said Florence. She hugged the ball. Dad clapped. Then Dad threw the beanbag, and it bounced off the rim and landed on the dog's head. The dog woke up and ran in a circle. Florence laughed and laughed. She threw the beanbag one more time. It sailed right through the hoop.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Jules was hungry. He wanted a snack. Grandma said, "Let's bake bread."

Jules watched with his eyes. Grandma mixed flour and water in a big bowl. Her hands went round and round. Then she put the dough near the warm stove to rise. "Can I touch it?" asked Jules. "Not the stove," said Grandma. "The stove is hot. But you can touch the dough later."

Soon the dough grew big. It looked like a soft cloud. Jules tapped the top with one finger. "Knock, knock," he said. The dough was squishy. His hands felt it. It was warm and soft like a pillow.

Then Grandma put the bread in the oven. Jules heard a click. He heard the oven hum. A yummy smell came out. Jules smelled it with his nose. "What is that smell?" he asked. "It is our bread," said Grandma. "Smells can tell us dinner is coming."

The timer went ding. The bread was not late after all. Grandma took it out with big mitts. She cut a slice and gave Jules a small piece. He tasted it with his tongue. It was warm and good. "Bread!" said Jules. "More, please."

activity: starting the first day of school

Evan walked over slowly. He held out his red truck. "You can push it," Evan said. The boy wiped his eyes. He pushed the truck in the sand. The truck rolled down the sand hill. The boy laughed out loud. Evan laughed too.

Then more kids came to watch. The truck rolled again and again. Soon everyone was taking turns pushing it. A teacher smiled and sat nearby. Evan sat down in the warm light of the sun. One boy patted him on the back. "Push it to me," the boy called. Evan pushed the truck hard. It rolled right to his new friend's hands.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Milo was at Grandma's house. He wanted to find the red ball. He looked under the blue chair. No red ball there. He looked behind the green plant. No red ball there either.

"Grandma, where is my red ball?" asked Milo. "Let's look together," said Grandma. They looked and looked.

Then Milo heard a funny sound. Pop, pop, pop. The sound came from the kitchen. Milo and Grandma went to look. Grandpa was at the stove. He was making popcorn. Grandpa moved the pot and kept it safe.

"Your red ball rolled in here," said Grandpa. "It rolled right under the yellow table." Milo hurried over. He got down on his knees. He reached under the yellow table. There it was! His red ball. It was smooth and warm from the sunny room.

"Thank you, Grandpa!" said Milo. He gave his grandpa a big hug. Then he saw the popcorn. It was white and fluffy, not red or blue or yellow. "Popcorn for you," said Grandpa. He put some in a small bowl.

Milo sat on the blue chair. He hugged his red ball. He munched the popcorn. The popcorn was all gone. "All gone!" said Milo. Grandma laughed. "Time for your nap," she said. Milo yawned a big yawn. He held his smooth red ball. He closed his eyes. "Sweet dreams, Milo," said Grandma.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Elizabeth wanted to wear her bear pajamas. But where were they? "Let's look," said Mommy.

First Elizabeth checked the bathtub. No pajamas there. The tub was empty now. Her bath was all done. Next she checked her chair. No pajamas there. Only a plate with crumbs. Her dinner was all done too. One place left to look.

Elizabeth ran to the big basket. There they were! The bear pajamas were waiting in the wash. "Can I have them?" she asked. Mommy said, "They are wet, so let's make them dry." Mommy put them in the dryer. Elizabeth watched the round door spin around and around.

At last the pajamas came out, warm and soft. Elizabeth pulled them on. She could zip the zipper all by herself. Then Mommy tucked her into bed. "One kiss for bear," said Elizabeth. "And one for me." Mommy kissed each sleepy eye. "Good night, safe and warm," Mommy said. Elizabeth hugged her bear tight.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Iris wants to wear her dress at school. But her dress is at home. It is in the wash. "Who will bring it to me?" she asks her teacher. "Your mama will bring it after lunch," says the teacher.

At lunch, Iris eats her crunchy carrots. Crunch, crunch, crunch. She drinks her milk. Then the door opens. It is Mama! She holds a small bag. Iris peeks inside. There is her clean dress. It smells like soap. The wash made it clean and soft.

Iris changes into her dress. The teacher helps her. "Now I have my dress on," says Iris. "Wash, wash, wash," she sings. "The wash made my dress new again!" She spins around and around. Her dress flutters like a butterfly.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Leo stood on the balcony with a big red pot. He wanted to grow tomatoes. His friend Mia lived next door. She grew tomatoes on her balcony too.

Leo put dirt in the pot. He made a little hole. He dropped in one seed. He patted the dirt down. Then he watered it with his small can.

Every morning Leo looked. Nothing came up. "Where is my tomato?" he asked.

Mia laughed. "Mine was little too. Then it grew tall."

Leo kept watering his pot. One morning he saw something green. A tiny sprout peeked out of the dirt. Leo clapped his hands.

The sprout grew and grew. It became a tall green plant. Round orange tomatoes hung on it. Leo picked one. It was warm from the sun.

He held it out to Mia over the wall. "A tomato for my friend!"

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Alexis was at Grandma's house. Mom came in with a little bundle. "This is your baby sister, Rose," said Mom. Alexis looked at Rose. She was tiny. She had little fingers and little toes.

Rose started to cry. She cried loud. "Wah, wah, wah." Alexis put his hands over his ears. "She is loud for someone so small," said Grandpa with a smile. "That is not a mean sound. That is how she talks." Alexis wanted her to stop. He wanted to be a good big brother.

Alexis found a rattle in the toy box. He shook the rattle near Rose. Shake, shake, shake. Rose stopped crying. She looked at the rattle. Her eyes got big. Alexis shook it again. Rose made a small gurgle. It sounded a bit like a giggle.

"That works!" said Grandma. "You found her favorite sound." Alexis felt proud. He shook the rattle slow. Rose watched it go back and forth. Her eyes followed every shake. She did not cry at all.

Then Alexis tried one more thing. He made a funny face, with his tongue out. Rose copied him! Her little tongue came out too. Mom laughed. "She is learning from you," said Grandma. "You are her first teacher." Alexis puffed up his chest. He shook the rattle one more time. Rose grabbed it with her whole tiny hand.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Aaron sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to help make cookies. Grandma said, "First, tell me your five senses."

Aaron tapped his head. "Ears?" Grandma smiled. She shook a little bell. Ring, ring! Aaron covered his ears. "My ears hear the bell!"

"That's one," said Grandma. "Now what else?"

Aaron picked up a cookie from a plate. It was warm. Grandma had taken it from the oven, not Aaron. He sniffed it with his nose. "My nose smells it. It smells sweet!"

"Good," said Grandma. "Keep going."

Aaron touched the cookie. "My fingers feel it. It is warm." He looked at it. "My eyes see it. It has chips!" He bit it. "My mouth tastes it. Yum!"

Grandma laughed. "You said all five. But wait. Where does the nose go?"

Aaron pointed to his ear. Then he stopped. "That is wrong. The nose goes here!" He touched his nose.

Grandma gave him the answer with a hug. "Five senses, five body parts. You did it."

The bell rang again. Aaron shouted, "I hear it with my ears!"

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Jasper wanted the red truck. Tom had the red truck. Tom would not give it up.

Miss Lily stood by the toy shelf. She sang a little song. "One, two, three," she sang. "Four, five, six." Tom held the truck tight. "Seven, eight, nine." Tom looked up. "Ten!" said Miss Lily. "Now it is Jasper's turn." Tom gave Jasper the truck. It was his turn to play.

Jasper pushed the truck on the floor. Vroom, vroom. He heard Miss Lily count again. "One, two, three," she sang to the block corner. Sam put down the blocks. He waited for his turn.

Then Jasper saw Miss Lily look at him. She held up her hand. She began to count. "One, two, three, four, five." Jasper stopped the truck. He rolled it back to Tom. "Your turn," said Jasper. Tom smiled and took the truck. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten," sang Miss Lily softly.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Zoe sat in the big chair at the clinic. Her mom held her hand. A friendly nurse came in with a small tray.

"Will the shot hurt?" Zoe asked.

"Just a little pinch," said the nurse. "Then we press a cotton ball on it."

The nurse opened a paper packet. She took out a little cotton ball. She wiped Zoe's arm with it. The cotton felt cold and wet.

Zoe watched the nurse's hands. The nurse tapped Zoe's arm up and down. Then the nurse gave the shot. Zoe felt one quick pinch. "Ouch!" said Zoe. But it was already done.

"Now you press," said the nurse. She put the cotton ball in Zoe's hand. Zoe pressed the cotton on her arm. She held it there and counted. "One, two, three."

Then Zoe took the cotton off. The little red spot did not bleed. "I pressed it and it stopped!" said Zoe.

"Yes, you did that yourself," said Mom. The nurse gave Zoe a shiny star sticker. Zoe put it on her shirt.

On the way out, they walked past the window. Zoe saw a garden with yellow flowers outside. "Can we look?" she asked.

Mom opened the door, and they stepped out into the sun.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxson wanted to wear his bear pajamas. But they were in the wash. "Oh no," said Jaxson.

Mama said, "First we finish dinner. Then a bath. Then clean pajamas."

Jaxson ate his noodles. All gone! Then Mama ran the bath. The water was warm, not hot. Mama checked it with her hand.

Jaxson splashed and played. He washed his tummy. He washed his toes.

Then Mama pulled the plug. The water went down, down, down. "Bye-bye, water," said Jaxson.

Mama said, "Now let's check the dryer." They looked in together. The bear pajamas were warm and dry! The wash had gone round and round. Then the dryer had made them dry.

Jaxson put them on. He looked like a little bear. "Rawr!" he said.

Papa came in and laughed. "A bear in my kitchen! I will call the zoo."

"No, Papa," said Jaxson. "This bear stays here."

Mama tucked him into bed. She read one story. The little bear closed his eyes.

"Sweet dreams, tidy little bear," Mama said. Jaxson snuggled down, warm and dry.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Zoe sat in the waiting room with her mom. Today she would get a shot. Zoe did not want a shot. She held her teddy tight.

"Will it hurt a lot?" she asked.

"Just a tiny pinch," said Mom. "Then we can skip to the car."

A nurse named Rosa came in. She had a special bottle of bubbles. Rosa rubbed Zoe's arm with a cool, wet cotton ball. It felt cold and soft.

"Watch the bubbles," said Rosa. She blew one big bubble. Zoe watched it float up. While Zoe watched, Rosa gave the shot.

"Done!" said Rosa.

Zoe looked down. There was a small round bandage on her arm. The bubbles had floated away, and the shot was already over.

"Can we do bubbles at my class tomorrow?" Zoe asked.

Mom laughed and kissed her head. "First, let's go skip to the car."

Zoe picked up teddy. She waved to Rosa. Then she skipped out the door.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Xavier wants to draw a big sun at school. Miss Ana gives him a tablet. It is dark and sleepy.

Xavier presses the round button. The screen lights up. He claps his hands. The picture is bright now.

He taps one more time. A drawing app opens. There is a green crayon on the screen. Xavier taps the green crayon. He draws a big green sun. "The sun is green," he says.

Ben sits next to him. Ben taps a blue crayon. "Look, blue," says Ben. Xavier taps the blue crayon too. Now his sun has blue rays.

Time to go outside. Miss Ana says, "Let's put the tablets away." Xavier presses the top button. The screen goes dark again. One press made it bright. One press made it sleepy. He puts the tablet in the basket.

"You did it all by yourself," says Miss Ana. Xavier smiles and waves to the dark screen. "Bye bye, tablet," he says.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Arya went to the library with Dad. She wanted a book about trucks. But the truck book was gone from its shelf.

"Let's look for shape clues," said Dad. He pointed at the book covers. "This one is a square. It has four sides, all the same." Arya patted the square cover. It felt big and flat.

They walked past the windows. The sun made bright patches on the floor. One patch was round like a circle. Arya put her shoe in the circle. It fit! She jumped to the next patch. That one had three sides. "Triangle!" she said. Dad smiled.

Then Arya saw a long, tall book on the reading table. Its cover was a rectangle, long on two sides and short on the others. She opened it. "Trucks!" she said. It was the truck book after all. A boy had left it on the table. "Thank you, book," Arya whispered. She sat down next to Dad.

Dad read about the big wheels. "The wheels spin," he said. Arya turned the page. The truck in the picture had a sharp pointy crane. "Beep beep!" said Arya, and she hugged the book tight.
